title: Calm and untroubled
core: All four mean nothing is stirring — no ripple, no agitation, no disturbance. What separates them is *what* is undisturbed and how the writer feels about it: a visible face or sky, a whole setting, a surface that nothing can ruffle, or a process that has simply stopped for now. Approval is not shared either — one is admiring, one is warm, one is double-edged, one is coolly indifferent. And only one of them implies the calm is temporary.

words.nuance: The only one with dignity — calm that is *displayed*, unclouded and faintly luminous, which is why it survives in **Your Serene Highness**. It's also the group's word for composure held while things go badly: a serene face in a collapsing room. Nobody is ever serene by accident.

The scene-setter: it attaches to places and moments — a village, a lake at dusk, an afternoon — far more readily than to a person under strain. It implies nothing ever disturbed the thing, so it can't describe calm recovered after an upset, and it is always warm and approving.

The only one that can be an insult. It describes a surface nothing ruffles — water, a face, a disposition — with no claim about inner life, so unflappable slides straight into unexcitable, incurious, bovine. If the sentence sounds faintly condescending about a person, this is the word.

Not a mood at all — it rates *activity*, not feeling, and can take a volcano, a tumour, a market, a feud. Uniquely it means paused rather than peaceful: the thing is expected back. Clinical and cold; a quiescent disease is nobody's idyll.

exam_note: Sentence equivalence loves pairing these as if interchangeable — decide on the noun (a place → tranquil, a process that will resume → quiescent) and the writer's attitude (admiring → serene, faintly dismissive → placid).
